explanations.explanation: Yep. The text says this was after King Jeconiah, the queen mother, the court officials, the craftsmen and the metalsmiths had been exiled from Jerusalem (Jeremiah 29:2). The king was already in Babylon when this letter went out. Even the king made that trip, friend.

Not quite, baker. Verse 2 says this was after King Jeconiah had been exiled from Jerusalem. He's in the list with the queen mother, the court officials, the craftsmen and the metalsmiths. So the king was already gone before the letter was written.

That's the one. The text says Zedekiah king of Judah sent Elasah and Gemariah to King Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon (Jeremiah 29:3). So Jeremiah's letter got to travel along on a king's errand. Free shipping, friend.

Close on the title, baker, but Josiah isn't the name in this verse. The text says Zedekiah king of Judah sent Elasah and Gemariah (Jeremiah 29:3). Lots of kings of Judah, so I get why the name was tempting.

Jeconiah shows up in the verse before this one, so it makes sense that his name stuck. But verse 2 lists him among the people already exiled from Jerusalem. The text says Zedekiah king of Judah sent Elasah and Gemariah to King Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 29:3).

Right on the money. The letter says, “This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says to all the exiles…” (Jeremiah 29:4). Jeremiah is the one writing, but these words are the LORD's. That tells you how much weight this letter carries.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is the one who carried these people into exile (Jeremiah 29:1). But he isn't the speaker here. The letter opens with “This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says…” (Jeremiah 29:4). Different Voice entirely, friend.

The priests are in the letter, but as people receiving it, along with the elders and the prophets (Jeremiah 29:1). The words come from somewhere higher. Verse 4 says, “This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says…” So the priests are on the mailing list, not the byline.

Not this time, baker. The LORD says, “Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce.” (Jeremiah 29:5). Nobody plants a garden while standing by the door with a suitcase. That instruction is about staying put.

That's right. Instead of packing, the exiles hear, “Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce.” (Jeremiah 29:5). Houses and gardens are not bag-packing words. A garden takes time, and that's the point.

Other way around, baker. The LORD says, “Take wives and have sons and daughters.” (Jeremiah 29:6). He goes on to say to take wives for their sons and give their daughters in marriage. So marriage and children are exactly what He tells them to do.

Correct. The LORD says, “Take wives and have sons and daughters.” (Jeremiah 29:6). He even says to take wives for their sons and give their daughters in marriage, so that they too may have sons and daughters. Families are meant to grow, even in Babylon.

That's it. The text says, “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles.” (Jeremiah 29:7). The LORD tells them to look for that city's good. Quite an instruction for people who didn't pick the address.

I can see how that might sound reasonable, baker, but it's not what the text says. The word is prosperity: “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles.” (Jeremiah 29:7). The LORD points them toward the city's good, not its downfall.

Good guess, but not the word in the verse. The text says, “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles.” (Jeremiah 29:7). The LORD isn't telling them to seek the city's leaders. What they're to seek is its prosperity.

explanations.answer: Because if it prospers they will too
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD says to pray to Him on the city's behalf, “…for if it prospers, you too will prosper.” (Jeremiah 29:7). Their good and the city's good are tied together. Pray for the neighbors, and the neighbors' good lands on you too.

explanations.answer: Because its king will set them free
explanations.explanation: That's not in the verse, baker. The reason the LORD gives is, “…for if it prospers, you too will prosper.” (Jeremiah 29:7). Nothing here says anything about the king freeing them. I'd stick with what the verse gives us.

explanations.answer: Because its people will join them
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that, friend. The LORD says to pray for the city, “…for if it prospers, you too will prosper.” (Jeremiah 29:7). The people joining them isn't mentioned. The reason is about their own prospering.

Careful there, baker. The LORD says, “Do not be deceived by the prophets and diviners among you, and do not listen to the dreams you elicit from them.” (Jeremiah 29:8). So it's a warning against listening, not an invitation. Those dreams are not the voice to trust.

Right. The LORD says, “Do not be deceived by the prophets and diviners among you, and do not listen to the dreams you elicit from them.” (Jeremiah 29:8). The exiles are told to stop listening. A dream that sounds nice isn't the same as a word from the LORD.

That's it. The LORD says they are falsely prophesying in His name: “…I have not sent them, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 29:9). Using His name doesn't mean He sent them. A name on the label doesn't tell you what's in the box.

explanations.answer: He sent them to test His people
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, baker. The LORD says, “…I have not sent them, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 29:9). So there's no sending at all, test or otherwise.

explanations.answer: They will be proven right later
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what the verse says. The LORD says they are falsely prophesying in His name, and “I have not sent them, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 29:9). Nothing here promises they'll turn out right.

Yes, baker. The exiles were carried away from Jerusalem (Jeremiah 29:1), and the LORD promises, “I will restore you to the place from which I sent you into exile.” (Jeremiah 29:14). The seventy years have an end, and the way home is part of the promise.

Not Egypt, friend. These exiles were carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon (Jeremiah 29:1). The LORD promises, “I will restore you to the place from which I sent you into exile.” (Jeremiah 29:14). That puts the destination back at Jerusalem.

Nineveh is the city Jonah was sent to (Jonah 1:2), but it's not part of this promise. The exiles were carried from Jerusalem to Babylon (Jeremiah 29:1). The LORD says, “I will restore you to the place from which I sent you into exile.” (Jeremiah 29:14).

explanations.answer: Prosper them and not harm them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says He knows the plans He has for them, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope.” (Jeremiah 29:11). That's what He says to people living in exile. Keep that line close.

That's not what the verse says, baker. The LORD says, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope.” (Jeremiah 29:11). Testing and humbling aren't in there. Prospering is.

Big dreams, friend, but the verse doesn't go there. The LORD says the plans are “to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope.” (Jeremiah 29:11). Nothing about ruling Babylon. I'd say a future and a hope is plenty.

That's right. The LORD says, “Then you will call upon Me and come and pray to Me, and I will listen to you.” (Jeremiah 29:12). Someone is listening on the other end. That's the LORD's own word to the exiles.
This one's true, baker. The LORD says, “Then you will call upon Me and come and pray to Me, and I will listen to you.” (Jeremiah 29:12). He says it plainly. The exiles can call and He will listen.

explanations.answer: When they search with all their heart
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD says, “You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart.” (Jeremiah 29:13). The finding comes with searching all the way. Half-hearted won't do it.

That's not in the verse, friend. The LORD says, “You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart.” (Jeremiah 29:13). Sacrifices aren't mentioned here. The searching is what's named.

explanations.answer: When a new prophet shows up
explanations.explanation: Hold on, baker. Just a few verses earlier the LORD warned them not to be deceived by the prophets among them (Jeremiah 29:8). Here He says, “You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart.” (Jeremiah 29:13). A new prophet isn't the condition.

That's right. The LORD says He will restore them from captivity and “gather you from all the nations and places to which I have banished you, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 29:14). All the nations and all the places. Nobody's left out of that gathering.

This one's true, baker. The LORD says, “I will restore you from captivity and gather you from all the nations and places to which I have banished you, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 29:14). He names every place He sent them. He promises to gather them from all of it.
